evidence: src/presentation/handlers/PayrollController.ts: submit() hands off to this.payroll.submitHours(...) and returns only { id: sheet.id }
src/presentation/handlers/PayrollController.ts: approve() hands off to this.payroll.approve(timesheetId) and returns { approved: sheet.approved }; it makes no approval decision itself

src/presentation/handlers/PayrollController.ts: submit()/approve() call this.audit.log(actor, ...) — coordination at the controller level that hands off to the business PayrollAuditService; it holds no audit logic itself
parsedVerdict.reasoning: PayrollController (presentation) only does presentation work. It defines the request shape (`HoursPayload`), turns request parameters into calls to the business services `PayrollService` and `PayrollAuditService`, and shapes the responses: `{id}`, `{approved}`, and the export text built with the view helper `payslipRow`. It holds no payroll calculations, validation rules, state changes, persistence or SQL. It also does not decide whether a timesheet can be approved. The one point you could argue about: the controller itself pairs each business call with `audit.log(actor, ...)`. That means the policy "every submit and approve must be audited" lives in the presentation layer and could be skipped by another entry point. Still, this is thin coordination that passes the caller's identity (the actor from the request context) to a business service. It is not a business rule computed or enforced in this file, so it is not a clear rubric violation. No ADR prose was provided.
